routes.description: Defend Catholic theism by reconciling uneven revelation, nonbelief, hell, inherited disorder, and suffering with universal grace, providence, and meaningful creaturely agency.
routes.successCriteria: Establish that God offers sufficient grace while differentiated circumstances, temporally extended revelation, free resistance, original sin, and formative suffering can explain apparent hiddenness without denying divine goodness.

motionBridge.description: Show that the disputed phenomena remain compatible with Catholic claims about universal grace, divine goodness, providence, and creaturely agency.

centralBridges.description: Explain how salvation and relationship with God remain genuinely available despite unequal cultural and evidential conditions.
Account for persistent nonbelief and damnation through meaningful creaturely resistance rather than divine refusal of relationship.
Connect original sin to present disorder without treating inherited deprivation as inherited personal guilt.
Explain how delayed disclosure and suffering can belong to a larger providential process of growing receptivity.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish gratuitous and differentiated divine gifts from an entitlement to identical temporal circumstances.
Supply theological and canonical interpretive principles for Genesis and Job rather than relying on isolated surface details.

routes.description: Argue that religious geography, sincere nonbelief, eternal consequences, inherited suffering, and unanswered suffering count against Catholic theism's account of divine love and providence.
routes.successCriteria: Establish that the observed distribution and persistence of nonbelief, together with morally arbitrary salvation conditions and inherited harms, are difficult to reconcile with a God able and willing to provide universal relationship and salvation.

motionBridge.description: Show that the disputed phenomena conflict with or are less expected under Catholic theism than under explanations without providential revelation.

centralBridges.description: Connect culturally patterned religious belief to a sociological explanation and challenge claims of universally accessible revelation.
Establish that sincere seekers can remain involuntarily unconvinced despite an alleged divine desire for relationship.
Show how contingent opportunities, cognitive limits, and eternal consequences create apparent arbitrariness or unfairness.
Challenge whether ancestral deception or refusal can justly explain deprivation and suffering borne by descendants.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Press the tension between providentially arranged conversion opportunities and the preservation of meaningful creaturely freedom.
Test formative interpretations of suffering against scriptural portrayals of divine conduct and compassion.

sections.title: Religious geography and fairness
sections.rationale: The accessibility and distribution of revelation directly bear on whether Catholic theism can reconcile universal salvific intent with unequal religious circumstances.

sections.title: Sincere nonbelief and salvation
sections.rationale: Whether conviction and salvation remain available to sincere seekers is central to the relationship among grace, cognitive limitation, freedom, and eternal consequences.

sections.title: Providence, contingency, and agency
sections.rationale: The debate requires an account of whether culturally mediated opportunities can be providential without making salvation arbitrary or compromising creaturely agency.

sections.title: Original sin and inherited deprivation
sections.rationale: Original sin supplies the Catholic explanation of disordered agency, while its initiating culpability and transmission determine whether present deprivation can be justified.

sections.title: Delayed revelation and formative suffering
sections.rationale: The personal case of sustained seeking and the dispute over Job test whether apparent silence and suffering can form receptivity within a loving providential order.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-01.proposition: Christian commitments make salvation and relationship with Christ universally available through many dimensions of ordinary human life.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-05.proposition: Human equality is not the governing standard of divine justice, because creation is gratuitous and differentiated natural gifts may be complemented by supernatural goods.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-07.proposition: Human freedom is limited but meaningful, and divine revelation may be recognized only across the extended narrative of a life through patient interpretation and perseverance.

chunk-002:c002-02.proposition: Persistent nonbelief can involve free rejection of an offered sequence of graces, while salvation always originates in grace and damnation in creaturely refusal.

chunk-002:c002-07.proposition: The evidential force of religious geography cannot be inferred from believer counts alone because cultural obstacles, institutional effects, and costly conversions require detailed empirical study.

chunk-002:c002-09.proposition: Providence offers recurrent opportunities for grace rather than controlling one decisive event, while human resistance and the inherited disorder of original sin explain failures to receive them.

chunk-002:c002-10.proposition: Original sin is the first rational creatures' rejection of their gifted dependence on God, causing loss of grace, integrated powers, immortality, and impassibility without changing human nature itself.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-08.proposition: Original sin is inherited as human nature deprived of superadded grace, not as an added guilty defect, while Adam represents humanity as its origin and best-equipped member and restoration remains personally available in salvation.

chunk-004:chunk-004-c02.proposition: Persistent questioning may progressively enlarge a person's capacity to recognize and receive an answer, even when divine response initially takes the form of deeper questions rather than a direct solution.

chunk-004:chunk-004-c04.proposition: Read canonically through the New Testament, divine questioning can provoke the very insight needed for revelation, while suffering may create capacities through which a larger providential story becomes visible.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-02.proposition: The geographic distribution of religious belief is better explained by human sociology than by a God proactively seeking relationship with everyone.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-04.proposition: Even without a best possible world, unequal access to revelation appears unfair when those differences may determine whether people receive eternal life.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-06.proposition: A sincere seeker cannot simply choose conviction, so making eternal destiny depend on cognitive limitations or unpersuasive arguments creates a hiddenness-based problem of evil.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-08.proposition: A lifelong journey cannot secure a hiddenness defense when another person's free action can abruptly end the seeker's opportunity and fix an eternal outcome.

chunk-002:c002-06.proposition: Religious geography makes conversion radically harder for some, whereas the observed cultural variation of religion is more expected if religions are human products.

chunk-002:c002-08.proposition: If salvation depends on contingent social encounters and trivial choices, outcomes appear arbitrary; if God arranges those encounters, providence threatens freedom and still leaves unequal intervention unexplained.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-02.proposition: The Eden account makes inherited suffering morally troubling because the first humans appear already vulnerable, deceived, and possibly without the moral knowledge required for culpability.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-09.proposition: Even if one imagines oneself in Adam's position, deception by a uniquely intelligent evil agent would not justify condemning the deceived person, much less that person's descendants.

chunk-003:chunk-003-candidate-10.proposition: O'Connor's sustained theological study, worship attendance, attempted prayer, and openness to others' prayers constitute extensive seeking, yet he reports receiving no discernible divine response.

chunk-004:chunk-004-c03.proposition: The Book of Job appears to portray God as inflicting suffering for a wager and then rebuking the sufferer for seeking an explanation, which conflicts with divine love and compassion.
